method: Data answers from answers/data_answers.py (data-answers.json): strict History PhDs 2009-2026 (n=1,303). Engagement = citing two or more anchor people of a group. Placement test = share of a person's citing PhDs that engage each candidate group, with lift over the group's base rate. Convention answers follow the atlas (historiography-1920-2000.json, GRAPH-FORMAT.md). Verification answers come from answers/verification.json once complete. 'user' marks questions the evidence cannot settle. 'research' answers come from the background research files in answers/research/ (2026-10-12).

answers.answer: Yes, a checked critique exists. Clarence Karr, 'What Happened to Canadian Intellectual History?', Acadiensis 18:2 (1989): 158-74, read in full, attacks the field's search for a national mind, its framing of everything as crisis and 'its narrow, elitist, biographical methodology' (p. 160): group biographies of 'an elite group composed primarily of academics, journalists and clergymen' (p. 169). Susan Mann Trofimenkoff (Canadian Literature 83, 1979: 7-20, read in full) had argued earlier that a field tied to nationalism had left women 'virtually non-existent'. Wright (Acadiensis 1995) names representativeness as the commonest charge against the field. Gauvreau 2010 is known only from a review. Palmer's Descent into Discourse is a general critique of poststructuralism, not checked against Canadian intellectual history. Owram 1989 is a self-assessment, not a critique. Each critique is cited by 0-5 of 1,303 PhDs, so they mark a debate, not current reading.
answers.change: Add a critique sentence anchored on Karr 1989 and Trofimenkoff 1979, with a critic row for Karr (check whether Trofimenkoff is already in the atlas). Do not use Palmer 1990 or Owram 1989 as critiques. Note the low uptake.

The francophone counterpart is Bienvenue and Dorais, eds., Profession historienne? (2023); Bienvenue 2018 shows Marie-Claire Daveluy foregrounding women in the history of New France. Laut, Abbott, Gérin-Lajoie and Cleverdon are not chapter subjects; Abbott and Gérin-Lajoie did not write Canadian history, and Wood-Legh wrote English history. Uptake is low except Neatby (16 PhDs) and Cleverdon (10).

Yes. Winona Stevenson (now Wheeler), 'Indigenous Voices, Indigenous Histories, Part I: The Othering of Indigenous History', Saskatchewan History 50:2 (Fall 1998): 24-27, read in full, addresses historians of 'Indian-White relations' and argues that relying on the records of one side keeps even agency-centred work 'within the colonialist framework' and others oral history; she is Cree (Fisher River Cree First Nation). LaRocque's 1999 dissertation (already an atlas source) criticises the 'neo cross-cultural approach' of Bailey, Jaenen, Trigger, Brown and Van Kirk as ethnological othering (PDF p. 249) and fur-trade historians' double standards (pp. 102, 109). Sioui 1989 critiques conventional history in general. Adams 1975 predates the field; Dickason worked within it. Trigger 1986 and Brownlie and Kelm 1994 are non-Indigenous context.
answers.change: Add Stevenson/Wheeler 1998 as a new source (replacing the unverified Wheeler placeholder) and Winona Wheeler (atlas id winona_wheeler) as a critic beside Sioui and LaRocque; add the pages read to the LaRocque claim. Do not present Adams or Dickason as critics of this field.

Heaman (best book 2018, Tax, Order, and Good Government: A New Political History of Canada; 53 citing PhDs overall), Tina Loo (2020; 109 citing PhDs overall), Heidi Bohaker (2021), Ivana Caccia (2011), Suzanne Morton (2015, with Mosby), Anne Trépanier (2025), and Lisa Pasolli and Jacqueline Briggs (articles). The profession's recent recognition centres a 'new political history' of state, tax and governance; the citation-based anchors (Granatstein, Bothwell, English) represent the older diplomatic and political synthesis.

answers.answer: Keep her, as a historian in the British Columbia strand. Her British Columbia: A History (1958) closes the first era of BC historiography: Reimer's study of how BC history was written ends in 1958 because of it. She was CHA president in 1965; sources conflict on whether she was the first or second woman to hold the office. Her low current PhD uptake (7) reflects the book's age, not its place in the historiography; the atlas uses precursor and historian rows for such figures. Sources: Canadian Encyclopedia (CHA president 1965), https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/index.php/en/article/margaret-anchoretta-ormsby; UBC History, https://history.ubc.ca/former-members/margaret-anchoretta-ormsby/; Reimer, Writing British Columbia History, 1784–1958 (UBC Press, 2009/2010), https://ubcpress.ca/writing-british-columbia-history-1784-1958, which ends in 1958 with her book (Favrholdt's review, BC Studies 166, 2010); Governor General honours record, https://www.gg.ca/en/honours/recipients/146-5300 ('first woman president'); BC Book Look ('second female president'), https://bcbooklook.com/welcome-to-the-ormsby-review/. The first/second-woman conflict is unresolved. Settled 2026-10-12 from the CHA's own list of presidents (cha-shc.ca): Hilda Neatby was the first woman president (1962-63) and Ormsby the second (1965-66). The Governor General's 'first woman president' is wrong.
answers.change: Keep Ormsby in cdn_regional (BC strand) with role 'historian'. Add 'Ormsby 1958' to the date label and Reimer 2009 as a source. If her presidency is mentioned, call her the CHA's second woman president (1965-66), after Neatby (1962-63).
